summary:
Vigil is on-board health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions. Each crew member wears a wristband that sends heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, motion and cabin air readings once a second. Vigil learns each person's own usual range for every vital sign, by context (sleep, rest, exercise) and time of day, and raises a staged alert (Watch, Alert, Critical) with the reason and the next steps, without waiting for the ground.
Alerts come from rules and statistics. A small classifier names the pattern, and a language model writes the explanation, shown only if every number in it matches the alert.
The cabin CO₂ stream and the radiation page use real ISS data from NASA OSDR, and the CO₂ limit follows NASA-STD-3001. Crew vital signs are simulated. We also built a working wristband prototype that streams to the same system. Vigil is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does and how it works

Vigil is on-board health monitoring software for astronauts. Each crew member wears a wristband that sends heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, motion and cabin air readings once a second. Vigil rolls the seconds into minute values, works out the context (sleep, rest, exercise or not worn), and learns each person’s own usual range for every vital sign by context and time of day. A reading outside that range raises a staged alert: Watch, Alert or Critical. Fixed safety limits apply from the first minute, before any personal range is learned. Each alert shows the reading, the reason and the next steps.

Benefits and intended impact

A fixed threshold either misses a change that matters for one person or raises false alarms for another. A personal range catches a real change earlier and stays quiet during exercise. On a mission far from Earth the crew cannot wait for a doctor on the ground, so the alert, the explanation and the steps all come from on board.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Backend: Python, Litestar, PostgreSQL.
  • Web client: TypeScript, React, Next.js.
  • Models: an XGBoost classifier that names the pattern of an alert, and a language model (DeepSeek, through an OpenAI-compatible API) that writes the explanation.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose, nginx, Traefik.
  • Hardware proof of concept: a wristband on an ESP32-S3 with optical, skin-temperature, CO₂, pressure and motion sensors, with firmware in C++ (PlatformIO). It streams to the same system as the simulated crew.
  • Data: ISS cabin CO₂ and radiation dose from the NASA OSDR Environmental Data App, the NASA-STD-3001 CO₂ limit, and the open datasets PPG-DaLiA, sleep-accel and BIDMC.
  • An AI coding assistant (Claude Code) was used for parts of the code and documentation.

How it is creative

Vigil compares each person with themselves, not with a population. The AI is kept in a narrow role: rules and statistics raise every alert, and the language model’s explanation is shown only if every number in it matches the alert. Real and simulated devices send the same 32-byte frame, so the software cannot tell them apart.

What we considered

  • False alarms: none in 315 simulated person-days of normal data.
  • Honesty about data: crew vital signs and abnormal episodes are simulated, and the interface and documents say so.
  • Privacy: the language model receives no names or ids.
  • Missing data: a missing reading is never shown as a good one.
  • Safety: the steps in an alert are written by people, and Vigil is a prototype, not a medical device.
